sentences: From a small panel, a young girl looks straight back at us.
She wears a tall hat and is shown from the chest up, in front of a dark wall.
Take a moment and simply meet her gaze.
This is Portrait of a Young Girl, painted around 1465 to 1470 by the Flemish painter Petrus Christus.
In 1444 he bought citizenship in Bruges so that he could work there as a painter.
He is often seen as the leading painter in Bruges after the death of Jan van Eyck.
Look first at her eyes.
They are very slightly out of line with each other, and her eyebrows are faintly uneven too.
This small break from symmetry holds our attention.
Unlike many women in portraits of the time, she calmly faces the viewer.
Her face is pale, her forehead high and her neck long.
All of these features match the ideals of beauty at court in her day.
Her expression seems calm well beyond her young years.
Her tall hat is a hennin, a headdress in fashion at the Burgundian court, made of black velvet with a gold border and small pearls.
A black strap runs under her chin.
Such straps are rare in pictures of the period, and some scholars think the idea was borrowed from a man's hat.
Moving down to her chest, we see a blue dress trimmed with ermine.
Around her neck hangs a gold chain in three rows.
Now look behind her.
Below a greyish-brown wall runs a wooden wainscot.
Light enters from the left, and her hat casts a shadow on the wall.
Christus is credited with being the first to place a portrait sitter inside a real room.
The careful detail of fabric and ornament shows van Eyck's influence.
Yet Christus reduced the sense of volume and gave his forms a slender, elongated shape.
In late works like this, he preferred a calm, balanced, geometric composition to complicated effects of space.
We do not know who the girl was.
An inscription on the lost original frame suggested she belonged to the English Talbot family, but this has never been proven.
A small portrait of a French lady in a Medici inventory of 1492 is thought to be this picture.
The painting entered the Prussian royal collection in 1821, with the purchase of Edward Solly's collection.
Today it hangs in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin, and it is often counted among the most refined portraits of the Northern Renaissance.
Step back and meet the girl's eyes once more.
Is she studying us, or is she careful to reveal nothing at all?
